skills.name: Define heat capacity and specific heat capacity; measure c for a solid

note.text:
Heat capacity C of a body is the heat needed to raise its temperature by 1 K: C = Q/Δθ, in J/K.
Specific heat capacity c of a material is the heat needed to raise 1 kg of it by 1 K: c = Q/(mΔθ), in J/(kg·K).
So Q = mcΔθ.
Water has a high specific heat capacity, 4200 J/(kg·K): it warms and cools slowly and makes a good coolant.
Method of mixtures for a solid: heat the solid in boiling water, move it quickly to a known mass of water in a calorimeter, stir, and take the highest temperature. Then heat lost by the solid = heat gained by the water and calorimeter.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text:
By the end, you should be able to use Q = mcΔθ to find heat, mass, temperature change or specific heat capacity, and describe how c is measured for a solid.
Builds on: Lesson {1} (heat and temperature) and Form Three energy calculations.
Leads to: Lesson {4} (c for a liquid) and Lesson {5}, where heat changes the state instead of the temperature.

sections.heading: Two capacities
sections.text:
Heat capacity C is for a whole body: the heat needed to raise its temperature by {1} K. C = Q ÷ Δθ, measured in J/K. A big kettle of water has a larger heat capacity than a small cup.
Specific heat capacity c is per kilogram: the heat needed to raise {1} kg of a material by {1} K. c = Q ÷ (mΔθ), in J/(kg·K). It depends only on the material.
Rearranged: Q = mcΔθ.
Water has c = {4200} J/(kg·K), much higher than most materials ({900} for aluminium, {400} for copper). So water warms slowly, cools slowly, and carries away a lot of heat as a coolant in a car engine.

sections.heading: Measuring c for a solid
sections.text:
• Find the mass of the metal block, and of the water and the calorimeter.
• Heat the block in boiling water until it is at {100} °C.
• Transfer it quickly into the cool water in the calorimeter, and stir.
• Take the highest temperature reached.
Then heat lost by the block = heat gained by the water (and the calorimeter):
m_block × c × (θ_hot − θ_final) = m_water × {4200} × (θ_final − θ_cold).
Working quickly and lagging the calorimeter reduce heat lost to the room, which is the main source of error.

worked_example.problem: How much heat is needed to raise the temperature of {m} kg of copper, c = {c} J/(kg·K), by {dt} K?

cards.idea: Heat capacity C = Q/Δθ is for a whole body, in J/K; specific heat capacity c = Q/(mΔθ) is per kilogram, in J/(kg·K).
example: {2} kg of water: c = {4200} J/(kg·K), so C = {8400} J/K

cards.idea: Q = mcΔθ: heat = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change.
In the method of mixtures, heat lost by the hot body = heat gained by the cold one.
example: hot metal into cool water: m₁c₁(θ₁ − θ) = m₂c₂(θ − θ₂)

check.prompt: A {ms} kg metal block at {hot} °C is dropped into {mw} kg of water at {cold} °C. The final temperature is {fin} °C. Taking c for water as {4200} J/(kg·K) and ignoring the calorimeter, find c for the metal, in J/(kg·K).

misconceptions.explain: The water GAINS heat (its temperature rises) and the metal LOSES it.

solution: Heat gained by the water = {mw} × {4200} × ({fin} − {cold}) = {heatMC(mw, 4200, fin - cold)} J.
Heat lost by the metal = {ms} × c × ({hot} − {fin}) = {ms * (hot - fin)}c.
Heat lost = heat gained, so c = {heatMC(mw, 4200, fin - cold)} ÷ {ms * (hot - fin)} = {answer} J/(kg·K).

pick.q: What is the specific heat capacity of a material?
pick.r: The heat needed to raise the temperature of {1} kg of it by {1} K
w: The heat needed to raise the whole body by {1} K
The heat needed to melt {1} kg of it
The temperature it reaches when heated
e: That is heat capacity C, in J/K, which depends on how much of the material there is.
That is specific latent heat of fusion; melting happens at a constant temperature.
Specific heat capacity is an energy per kilogram per kelvin, not a temperature.
pick.y: 'Specific' means per kilogram: c = Q ÷ (mΔθ), in J/(kg·K).

pick.q: What is the heat capacity of a body?
pick.r: The heat needed to raise the temperature of that whole body by {1} K
w: The heat needed to raise {1} kg of it by {1} K
The total heat energy stored in the body
The highest temperature the body can reach
e: That is specific heat capacity, which is per kilogram and depends only on the material.
Heat capacity is about the heat needed for a rise of {1} K, not the energy already stored.
A body has no highest temperature of this kind; heat capacity is an energy per kelvin.
pick.y: C = Q ÷ Δθ, in J/K. A bigger body of the same material has a bigger heat capacity.

pick.q: What is the unit of specific heat capacity?
e: J/K is the unit of heat capacity, which is for a whole body.
J/kg is the unit of specific latent heat, where there is no temperature change.
The joule is the unit of heat itself, not of a capacity.
pick.y: c = Q ÷ (mΔθ): joules divided by kilograms and by kelvin.

pick.q: Water has a specific heat capacity of {4200} J/(kg·K) and copper {400} J/(kg·K). Which warms up faster for the same heat and mass?
pick.r: The copper, because less heat is needed for each degree
w: The water, because it has the larger value
They warm at the same rate
e: A large c means more heat is needed for each degree, so water warms more slowly.
The two values differ by more than ten times, so the rates differ greatly.
Both warm; the question is which warms faster.
pick.y: Δθ = Q ÷ (mc): the smaller the c, the bigger the temperature rise for the same heat.

pick.q: Why is water used as the coolant in a car engine?
pick.r: It has a high specific heat capacity, so it carries away a lot of heat for a small rise in temperature
w: It has a low specific heat capacity, so it heats up quickly
It conducts heat better than any metal
It never boils inside an engine
e: A low value would mean it heated quickly and carried away little heat.
Metals conduct far better than water; what matters here is the heat water can carry away.
Water can boil in an engine, which is why the system is kept under pressure.
pick.y: With c = {4200} J/(kg·K), each kilogram takes in {4200} J for every degree it rises.
